subject: chemistry
title: Infrared spectroscopy
key_idea: Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers. An IR spectrum shows which bonds, and so which functional groups, a compound contains.

blocks.text: Covalent bonds are not rigid. They stretch and bend all the time. This section covers why infrared radiation is absorbed and what an IR spectrum shows.

items.meaning: Electromagnetic radiation with a lower frequency than visible light, but one that matches the vibration of covalent bonds.
The number of waves per centimetre, in cm⁻¹. IR spectra are plotted against wavenumber.
The percentage of radiation that passes through the sample. A dip is an absorption.

items: A bond absorbs IR radiation when the radiation's frequency matches the bond's natural vibration frequency.
The bond then vibrates with more energy.
Each type of bond (O–H, C=O, C–H) absorbs at its own **characteristic wavenumber**, depending on the atoms and the bond strength.
The spectrum is a plot of transmittance against wavenumber. Each trough is an absorption by a bond.
A bond absorbs IR when the radiation's frequency matches the bond's vibration.
Different bonds absorb at different wavenumbers, so troughs identify bonds.

blocks.text: Use a data sheet to match each strong absorption to a bond. This section covers the bonds in the functional groups you need.

rows: Aldehydes, as well as the C=O

items: Almost every organic compound shows C–H absorption near 3000 cm⁻¹, so it does not help to tell them apart.
A strong, sharp peak at about 1700 cm⁻¹ shows **C=O**. Aldehyde, ketone, acid and ester all show it.
A broad peak at about 3300 cm⁻¹ shows an **alcohol** O–H.
A carboxylic acid has both C=O and a very broad O–H, which stretches under the C–H peaks.
A C=O peak with no broad O–H peak points to an aldehyde, ketone or ester.

diagram.alt: Pick a compound and see its main IR absorptions.

items.text: Write down every bond type in the molecule.
Find each bond's wavenumber range on the data sheet.
Note whether any O–H is broad, and whether any C=O is present.

items: Look first for the O–H region, then for C=O near 1700, then for C=C.
Broad O–H plus C=O means carboxylic acid.
Use ranges from the data sheet to name each peak.

blocks.text: Some gases in the atmosphere absorb IR. This section covers why that matters for climate.

items: Gases whose molecules contain **C=O**, **O–H** or **C–H** bonds absorb IR. Examples are CO₂, H₂O and CH₄.
The Earth's surface emits IR radiation. These gases absorb some of it before it escapes to space.
The absorbed energy is re-emitted in all directions, which warms the lower atmosphere.
Rising levels of these gases are linked to global warming. This is the main reason for efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and cut energy demand.
CO₂, H₂O and CH₄ absorb IR because their bonds vibrate.
More of these gases traps more heat.

checks.q: An IR spectrum has a strong peak at 1715 cm⁻¹ and a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹. Which functional group is present?
checks.a: A carboxylic acid: C=O at about 1700 cm⁻¹ and a very broad O–H.

checks.q: Explain why a molecule's bonds absorb infrared radiation.
checks.a: The frequency of the IR matches the natural vibration frequency of the bond. The bond absorbs the energy and vibrates more.

checks.q: Explain why methane is a greenhouse gas.
checks.a: Its C–H bonds absorb IR radiation emitted from the Earth's surface, which warms the atmosphere.

blocks.text: IR spectroscopy is used to monitor air quality and to test breath.

items: **Air pollution**: CO and NO from car exhausts absorb IR at known wavenumbers, so their amounts can be measured in the air.
**Breathalysers**: ethanol in the breath absorbs IR through its C–H and O–H bonds. The amount of absorption gives the concentration of ethanol.
In examinations, the IR absorption data are provided on the data sheet.

blocks.text: Spectra are used to identify bonds, to identify a substance and to spot impurities.

items: The part of the spectrum below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is the **fingerprint region**. It contains many absorptions unique to each molecule.
A sample is identified by comparing its whole spectrum with a database of known spectra.
A peak in the spectrum that does not belong to the pure compound shows an **impurity**. For example, a broad O–H absorption in a sample of an ester points to water or alcohol.
